Photoredox copper-catalyzed regioselective
syntheses of allenols via HAT-mediated propargyl
radical generation†
Wenyao Li,a Hao Yu
 *a and Shengming Ma
 *a,b
Selectivity control of the reactions of propargylic and/or allenylic radicals remains particularly elusive.
Here, a visible light-mediated Cu-catalyzed protocol for the highly selective syntheses of tri- and tetra-
substituted allenols from alkynol derivatives has been developed. The synthetic potential of the products
has been demonstrated. The control experiments, Stern –Volmer quenching, and cyclic voltammetry
studies support a reaction pathway involving the generation of allenyl radicals via photo-mediated N –O
bond scission, an intramolecular 1,5-HAT process, the resonance to propargylic radicals, and coupling. A
non-common intramolecular 1,6-HAT process has also been observed.
Introduction
Selectivity control is an everlasting topic in organic synthesis,
advanced materials, and medicinal chemistry or life science. 1
For example, it is of particular interest to see the chemistry on
the propargylic/allenylic species due to the versatile potential
of alkynes and allenes. Recently, much attention has been
paid to the generation and reactivity of propargylic and/or
allenylic radicals a ﬀording alkynes
2 and/or allenes. 3–6
However, the e ﬃcient generation of propargylic radicals and
the selectivity-controlled trapping still remain particularly
elusive (Fig. 1a). 1,5-Hydrogen atom transfer (HAT)
7,8 mediated
by alkoxyl radicals 9,10 has emerged as an important strategy
for C(sp 3)–H bond functionalization (Fig. 1b). Given the high
eﬃciency of radical formation with this specific method, we
wonder whether such an alkoxyl radical-induced HAT of
alkynes would e ﬃciently generate propargylic radicals followed
by transition metal-catalyzed functionalization, providing an
eﬃcient and selective platform for synthesizing multi-substi-
tuted alkynes or allenes (Fig. 1c). However, notable challenges
for such a concept included (Fig. 1c): firstly, the tautomeric
equilibrium of propargylic radicals to allenyl radicals and the
resulting control of selectivity for trapping of these two
radicals;
2–4 secondly, the introduction of the alkyne functional
group and the formation of the allene functional group may
lead to direct cyclic radical addition reactions; 11 and thirdly,
the facile HAT of allenyl radicals could produce other non-
functionalized allene by-products before the transition metal-

platform reaction for the study on how far a HAT reaction may
go. Here, we report our success on the exclusive synthesis of
tri- and tetra-substituted allenes via visible-light photoredox
and copper dual catalysis (Fig. 1d).
Results and discussion
Our initial attempt used N-alkynoxyphthalimide 1a, which is
easily obtained by the Mitsunobu reaction from the corres-
ponding alkynol. We began investigating the coupling reaction
of 1a with trimethylsilyl cyanide by applying a catalytic system
consisting of 4CzIPN and CuCl/dmbpy in CH 3CN under blue
LED irradiation, and the desired allene product 2a′ was
aﬀorded in 38% yield as determined by 1H NMR spectroscopy
(Table 1, entry 1), without the formation of an alkyne product.
The photocatalyst MesAcr +ClO4
− resulted in a largely
decreased yield of the allene product 2a′ (Table 1, entry 2).
Further exploration of photocatalysts revealed that iridium
complexes, such as Ir[(dtbbpy)( ppy) 2]PF6 or Ir( ppy) 3, were
more eﬃcient (Table 1, entries 3 and 4). Other copper catalysts
such as CuBr and CuI (Table 1, entries 5 and 6) were also
screened and CuCl was still the best. Subsequently, we tested a
series of other bipyridine ligands, and identified 1,10-phenan-
throline as equally excellent as dmbpy (Table 1, entry 7). We
chose 1,10-phen as the ligand of preference finally in consider-
ation of the price. Other alkynoxylamide derivatives, such as
3a and 4a, exhibited a much lower reactivity (Table 1, entries 8
and 9). Control experiments demonstrated that the CuCl/1,10-
phen system, photocatalyst and light are indispensable for
enabling this transformation to proceed smoothly (entries
10–12).
With the optimized conditions in hand, we conducted
further investigations on the substrate scope of this reaction
(Fig. 2). We found that a wide range of terminal alkynols are
suitable for this transformation, leading to the successful
preparation of the corresponding tri-substituted allenols 2a–2t
smoothly. In terms of the alkyl groups R

tion, non-functionalized linear primary alkyl chains of various

even a tertiary alkyl group ( 2q), resulting in the corresponding

alkyl-substituted substrates, the reaction of the substrate with
R1 as phenyl yielded 2r smoothly, achieving a yield of 66%.
Furthermore, the synthesis of secondary allenols 2s and 2t was
realized with yields of 76% and 60%, respectively. Finally, this
protocol also worked for internal alkynols with R 2 being alkyl,
phenylalkyl or phenyl groups, a ﬀording tetra-substituted alle-
nols (2u–2ae).
Furthermore, various N-alkynoxyphthalimide precursors
with diverse tether sizes were employed to investigate the
potential of our protocol for 1,4- or 1,6-HAT (Fig. 3). When sub-
jected to the standard conditions, compound 1af failed to
yield the corresponding beta-allenol 2af, with the complete
consumption of the starting material observed (Fig. 3a).
Conversely, the reaction of substrate 1ag with TMSCN resulted
in the formation of delta-allenol 2ag in 45% yield, involving
1,6-HAT. Furthermore, endeavors to synthesize the initial
N-alkynoxyphthalimide precursor for alpha-allenols proved
unsuccessful (see Fig. S4 in the ESI †).
To demonstrate the synthetic potential of this reaction, a
gram-scale reaction was conducted using 7 mmol of 1a, result-
ing in the formation of allenol 2a with an isolated yield of 73%
(1.1 g) (Fig. 4a). These allenols are versatile synthetic building
blocks as shown in Fig. 4b. In the presence of Cs
2CO3, allenol
2a underwent oxycyclization to give the dihydropyran product
5, which may further react with 4-chlorobenzyl bromide 12 to
produce the dihydropyran product 6 in a one-pot reaction. The

2a aﬀorded allenal 8 under the catalysis of 20 mol% each of Fe
(NO3)3·9H2O, TEMPO, and NaCl in DCE. 14 Meanwhile, under
the catalytic system of Fe(NO 3)3·9H2O, TEMPO, and KCl, 2a
was converted into carboxylic acid, which was further esterified
with TMSCHN 2 in one pot to provide allenoate 9 in 66% yield
over two steps. 15 Upon treatment with CBr 4 and I 2, the allenol
product 2a could be easily transformed into the synthetically
versatile allenyl bromide 10 and allenyl iodide 11,
respectively.16,17 Finally, 2a may readily undergo a Mitsunobu
reaction18 to aﬀord allenyne 12 in a decent yield.
To gain mechanistic insights into the reaction, firstly, we
conducted the reaction of 1a in the presence of radical trap-
ping agents such as TEMPO and BHT. As shown in Fig. 5a, the
yield of the desired allenols dropped dramatically with the
increase in the amount of the radical inhibitor. In addition,
when BHT was used, the alkynol product S1a, resulting from
intermolecular HAT of the initially formed alkoxyl radical, was
detected. When the internal alkyne 1ah substituted with the
triisopropylsilyl group was subjected to the standard con-
ditions, in addition to the normal allene product 2a, the iso-
lation of the tetrahydrofuranyl triisopropylsilyl acetylene
product 13ah indicated the involvement of a propargylic
cation, which may be formed via the oxidation of a propargylic
radical intermediate (Fig. 5b). Moreover, Stern –Volmer
quenching experiments (Fig. 5c) demonstrated that the CuCl/
1,10-phen catalyst, rather than the substrate 1a, quenched the
excited-state photocatalyst Ir( ppy)
3, suggesting a reductive
quenching pathway. The half peak potential of the catalyst
CuCl/1,10-phen Ered

determined to be −1.27 V vs. SCE in CH 3CN (Fig. 5d).
On the basis of these experimental results, a plausible reac-
tion mechanism was proposed (Fig. 6). Initially, the excitation
of the photocatalyst Ir( ppy) 3 leads to its excited state Ir*( ppy) 3
(Ered
1=2 [IrIII*/IrII] = +0.31 V vs. SCE in CH 3CN),19 which can be
reductively quenched with LCu ICN (Ered
p=2 [CuII/CuI] = +0.26 V vs.
SCE in CH 3CN) to generate LCu II(CN) and [Ir( ppy) 3]− species.
[Ir( ppy)3]− (Ered
1=2 [IrIII/IrII]= −2.19 V vs. SCE in CH 3CN)19 would
reduce substrate 1 (Ered
p=2 [1a/1a−] = −1.27 V vs. SCE), producing
radical anion intermediate I and regenerating the photo-
catalyst Ir( ppy)3. Subsequently, alkoxy radical intermediate II
would be generated via the cleavage of the N –O bond of inter-
mediate I. The subsequent intramolecular 1,5-HAT would
generate radical intermediate III. Mulliken atomic spin density
analysis suggests that intermediate III is a delocalized radical,
with the spin density distributed across both ends of the
system (0.763 at C1 and 0.487 at C2, with R 1 being n-hexyl and
R2 being methyl). Finally, intermediate III can be trapped by
the LCu II(CN)2 species, leading to the formation of the allene
product 2.
Conclusions
In summary, we have developed a unified platform for the
highly selective preparation of tri- and tetra-substituted alle-
nols. This approach leverages dual copper and photoredox cat-
alysis to enable the generation and functionalization of allenyl
radicals. This mild reaction demonstrates a broad substrate
scope, and the post-reaction transformations of the allenol
products highlight the significant synthetic potential of this
methodology.

Selectivity control of the reactions of propargylic and/or allenylic radicals remains particularly elusive.
Here, a visible light-mediated Cu-catalyzed protocol for the highly selective syntheses of tri- and tetra-
substituted allenols from alkynol derivatives has been developed. The synthetic potential of the products
has been demonstrated. The control experiments, Stern–Volmer quenching, and cyclic voltammetry
studies support a reaction pathway involving the generation of allenyl radicals <sub>v</sub>i<sub>a</sub> photo-mediated N–O
bond scission, an intramolecular 1,5-HAT process, the resonance to propargylic radicals, and coupling. A
non-common intramolecular 1,6-HAT process has also been observed.
Introduction

advanced materials, and medicinal chemistry or life science.
For example, it is of particular interest to see the chemistry on
the propargylic/allenylic species due to the versatile potential
of alkynes and allenes. Recently, much attention has been
paid to the generation and reactivity of propargylic and/or
allenylic radicals afording alkynes<sup>2</sup> and/or allenes.<sup>3–6</sup>

the selectivity-controlled trapping still remain particularly

for

Conclusions

In summary, we have developed a unified platform for the
highly selective preparation of tri- and tetra-substituted alle-
nols. This approach leverages dual copper and photoredox cat-
alysis to enable the generation and functionalization of allenyl
radicals. This mild reaction demonstrates a broad substrate
scope, and the post-reaction transformations of the allenol
products highlight the significant synthetic potential of this
methodology.
